title: [A2 • Band 4.0] Bài 307: The Evolution of Altruism
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 307 (LEVEL A2 • BAND 4.0)

The Evolution of Altruism: Beyond the Selfish Gene

Paragraph 1. For fifty years, many biology books taught a harsh idea about nature. In 1976, scientist Richard Dawkins wrote a famous book saying that every living creature acts mostly to protect its own genes. Under this old rule, even kind acts looked secretly selfish. Animals helped family members who shared their genes, or helped friends only to get help back later. Scientists thought true kindness toward strangers was impossible.

Paragraph 2. However, scientist Dr. Marcus Sterling challenges this cold picture in his new book. He agrees that individual survival matters, but says old science forgot the power of teamwork. Across many animal species, from underground mole-rats to ocean whales, cooperative groups survive better than lonely, selfish individuals. Early human tribes that shared food and defended one another easily beat selfish, divided groups.

Paragraph 3. Computer games also prove that kindness wins in the long run. Political scientist Robert Axelrod ran computer tests where players could cheat or cooperate. Purely selfish players who cheated everyone soon lost and failed. Fair players who started nicely and copied their partner stayed strong. Even better, when humans share food or help others, our brains release happy chemicals that create calm feelings and trust.

Paragraph 4. Finally, Dr. Sterling criticizes modern money systems for treating people as purely selfish. When schools and companies only reward personal competition, they push down our natural desire to help each other. Sterling concludes that humans survived history not through cruel power, but by trusting, working together, and caring for weak people.

groups.title: Questions 5–8
groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D.

steps: Đoạn 1: "...acts mostly to protect its own genes."
Đoạn 4: "When schools and companies only reward personal competition..."

q5.text: What did older biology books say about animals helping each other?
options: A. Only whales and rats show real kindness.
B. Helping strangers always helps animals live longer.
C. Even helpful acts were secretly done for selfish reasons.
D. Humans never shared food in early history.

steps: Đoạn 1: Sách cũ cho rằng mọi hành động tốt đẹp đều mang tính ích kỷ ngầm (bảo vệ gen hoặc đổi chác).

q6.text: What did Robert Axelrod's computer tests show?
options: A. Cooperating fairly beats pure selfishness over time.
B. Cheating other players is the safest way to win.
C. Computers cannot copy how humans make choices.
D. Animals are smarter than computer programs.

steps: Đoạn 3: Người ích kỷ gian lận sớm sụp đổ, người hợp tác công bằng giữ được sức mạnh lâu dài.

q7.text: What happens inside the human brain when people share?
options: A. People feel tired and lose energy quickly.
B. The brain stops paying attention to strangers.
C. Memory becomes weaker for several hours.
D. The body releases happy chemicals that reward kindness.

steps: Đoạn 3: Khi chia sẻ, não tiết ra chất hóa học tích cực tạo sự bình yên và tin tưởng.

q8.text: According to Dr. Sterling, how did humans survive through history?
options: A. By building big cities with strong walls
B. By working together and caring for weaker members
C. By letting the strongest individual rule alone
D. By competing in schools and businesses

steps: Đoạn 4: Loài người tồn tại nhờ tin tưởng, hợp tác và chăm sóc người yếu thế.
